questions.question: How is the adjugate matrix formed from cofactors?
options: Take the transpose of the cofactor matrix.
Divide the original matrix by its determinant.
Delete the first row and first column.

questions.question: For which matrices is the adjugate defined?
What is $\operatorname{adj}(I_n)$?
What role does the adjugate play for a nonsingular matrix?
options: It replaces the determinant by the trace.
It appears in the inverse formula $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{\det(A)}\operatorname{adj}(A)$.
It proves that every square matrix is singular.
It turns a matrix into an augmented matrix.

questions.question: Why is the transpose step important in the adjugate?
options: The transpose step deletes all cofactors.
The transpose step makes the matrix rectangular.
The adjugate is not just the cofactor matrix; it is its transpose.
The transpose step is needed only for diagonal matrices.

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$, what is $\operatorname{adj}(A)$?
Find $\operatorname{adj}\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$.
If $A=I_3$, what is $\operatorname{adj}(A)$?
If $A$ is nonsingular and $\det(A)=2$, which inverse formula is correct?
For $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$, what is $\operatorname{adj}(A)$?
What is the difference between the cofactor matrix and the adjugate matrix?
options: The adjugate is the transpose of the cofactor matrix.
The cofactor matrix is defined only for nonsingular matrices.
They differ only when the determinant is zero.
The adjugate is obtained by deleting all negative cofactors.

questions.question: Can a singular matrix have an adjugate?
options: Yes, and it always equals the inverse.
No, singular matrices have no cofactors.
Yes, but the inverse formula with $1/\det(A)$ cannot be used.
No, because the adjugate requires rectangular matrices.

questions.question: Why does the formula $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{\det(A)}\operatorname{adj}(A)$ require nonsingularity?
options: Because adjugates exist only when every entry is positive.
Because cofactors cannot be computed for singular matrices.

questions.question: Find $\operatorname{adj}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$.
For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$, use the adjugate formula to write $A^{-1}$.
If $\det(A)=0$, what remains true about $\operatorname{adj}(A)$?
options: $\operatorname{adj}(A)$ is defined, but the inverse formula fails.

questions.question: Why is calling the adjugate simply “the inverse without dividing” imprecise?
options: Built from transposed cofactors; enters the inverse formula only when $\det(A)\ne0$.
It is always a scalar, not a matrix.
It is never related to inverses.
It exists only after the inverse has been computed, in every case without exception.

questions.question: For a nonsingular matrix, what information is still missing if you know only $\operatorname{adj}(A)$ but not $\det(A)$?
options: The transpose operation, in all instances without exception.
The scalar factor $1/\det(A)$ in the inverse formula.

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$, what is $\operatorname{adj}(A)$?
A student computes the cofactor matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$. What is the adjugate?
